means: What is left from sales after product cost, shipping, payment fees, discounts, refunds and ads. This is the number Helix cares about most.
All the money customers paid. It looks good, but it is not what you keep.
Bills that stay the same each month, like rent, software, staff and your own wage.
Costs that grow with every order: product cost, shipping and payment fees.
What one item costs you to make or buy, including freight to your warehouse.
The share of each sale you keep after product cost. A $100 sale with $40 product cost is a 60% margin.
Average order value: total sales divided by number of orders.
Return on ad spend: how many dollars of sales you get for each $1 of ads. ROAS 3 means $3 of sales for $1 of ads.
The ROAS where an order makes $0 profit after its costs. Below it, ads lose money.
Cost per acquisition: how much ad money it took to get one sale.
The most you can pay in ads for one sale before that sale stops making money.
The cost per sale you aim for so each sale still leaves you profit.
All ad spend divided by all sales, as a percentage. MER 25% means $25 of ads for every $100 of sales.
Out of every 100 visits, how many end in an order. 2% means 2 orders per 100 visits.
One visit to your store. One person can make several visits.
Click-through rate: out of every 100 people who saw your ad, how many clicked.
Cost to show your ad 1,000 times.
How many times, on average, the same person saw your ad.
Out of everyone who saw your video ad, the share who watched at least 3 seconds. It tells you if the opening grabs attention.
A video view of 15 seconds or more (or the whole video if it is shorter).
The first line or first 3 seconds of an ad. Its only job is to make people stop scrolling.
The reason to buy that an ad focuses on, like saving time or looking good.
The ad itself: the picture or video plus the words.
Photos and videos made by real customers or creators instead of the brand.
A person who makes social content and can feature your product.
An ad that runs from a creator's own account, so people see their name instead of yours.
The top level in an ad account. It holds the goal, like getting sales.
The middle level in Meta. It holds who sees the ads, where, and often the budget.
The first days after you start or change an ad set, while Meta works out who to show it to. Results jump around, so wait.
A small piece of code on your store that tells Meta when someone views, adds to cart or buys.
Sales sent to Meta straight from your store's server, so fewer sales go untracked.
Tags added to the end of a link so your analytics can tell which ad or email a visitor came from.
People who have never heard of you.
People who know you: they visited, followed or watched your videos.
People close to buying: they added to cart or started checkout.
A list Meta builds from your own data, like site visitors or customers.
People Meta thinks are similar to a list you give it, like your best customers.
Letting Meta find buyers with few or no audience limits. Works best with strong ads.
Meta's automatic settings that let its system choose audience, placements or budget for you.
A Google campaign type that shows your products across Search, Shopping, YouTube and more from one campaign.
Ads that show when people search your brand name. Cheap and usually very profitable.
The list of your products, prices and photos that Google and Meta read to make shopping ads.
The exact words people typed into Google before they saw or clicked your ad.
A word you tell Google never to show your ads for, to stop wasted clicks.
The page someone lands on after clicking an ad.
The part of a page you see before you scroll.
The steps from seeing an ad to buying: visit, add to cart, checkout, order.
Out of every 100 visits, how many add something to the cart.
One-tap payment options like Apple Pay, Google Pay and Shop Pay.
Payment options like Afterpay or Klarna that let shoppers split the cost.
The order amount where shipping becomes free, like 'Free shipping over $100'.
Two or more products sold together, often with a small saving.
A one-click extra offer shown right after someone buys.
A clear promise that removes the fear of a bad purchase, like a 30-day money-back promise.
An email or text series that sends by itself when something happens, like a new sign-up.
A one-off email you send to your list, like a new arrival announcement.
A smaller group of your list, like people who bought in the last 90 days.
A box on your site that asks visitors for their email, often with a small reward.
When someone starts checkout but does not finish. A reminder email can bring them back.
How much a customer spends with you over time, not just on the first order.
How many weeks your stock will last at the current sales speed.
A week-by-week list of money coming in and going out, so you can see tight weeks early.
Changes that help your store show up in Google without paying for ads.
The short summary under your page title in Google results.
Deciding which ad or channel gets credit for a sale.
Turning something off for a while (or in one area) to see how many sales it really adds.
Key performance indicator: one of the few numbers you watch to know if things are working.
Unpaid: posts, search results and word of mouth that you do not pay to show.
